terms.definition: a model built from many small calculating units (neurons) arranged in layers; each layer's outputs are the next layer's inputs.
a neural network with many layers stacked between input and output ("deep" = many layers).
one step of a network: a group of neurons that all read the same inputs and pass their outputs on together.
one calculating unit: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the sum through an activation function.
a layer between the input and the output; you never see its outputs directly, only the next layer does.
the last layer; its outputs are the network's predictions (here: one probability per class).
a number on one connection between two neurons; the input is multiplied by it. Training is changing the weights. (Keras also calls weights parameters.)
one extra number per neuron, added to its weighted sum, so the neuron can shift its output up or down even when every input is 0.
what a neuron computes before its activation function: each input times its weight, all added up, plus the bias. The book calls it z.
the small function a neuron applies to its weighted sum before passing it on (sigmoid, ReLU ...). Without it, a stack of layers could only draw straight lines.
the S-shaped activation 1 / (1 + e^-z): squeezes any number into 0..1. Also called the logistic function.
the hyperbolic tangent: an S-shaped activation like sigmoid, but its outputs run from -1 to +1, centred on 0.
the rectified linear unit, max(0, z): passes positive sums unchanged and turns every negative sum into exactly 0.
an output-layer activation that turns the 10 raw scores into 10 probabilities that add up to 1, one per class.
the part of TensorFlow for building and training networks (imports start with tf.keras).
Google's library for deep learning: fast arithmetic on big grids of numbers, plus automatic gradients.
Keras's simplest kind of model: a plain list of layers, each feeding the next.
a layer in which every neuron is connected to every input (tf.keras.layers.Dense). Dense(100) = 100 neurons.
a layer that turns each 28 x 28 image into one row of 784 numbers, because a Dense layer reads rows.
Keras's name for a layer's weight matrix, as in kernel_initializer. Not the similarity kernel of Chapter 2: same word, different thing.
choosing the random numbers the weights start at, before any training step.
the number of inputs one neuron of a layer receives (fan-out: the number of outputs the layer produces; fan_avg = their average).
random numbers spread evenly between a low and a high limit: every value in the range is equally likely.
the bell curve of Chapter 2 (Gaussian), described by its mean and its spread; he_normal draws starting weights from one.
start each weight at random with variance 1 / fan_avg; Keras's default. Suits sigmoid, tanh, softmax or no activation.
start each weight at random with variance 2 / fan_in: twice as spread out, because ReLU throws away the negative half. Suits ReLU and its variants.
start each weight at random with variance 1 / fan_in; the one SELU needs.
for every weight, one number saying how much the loss would change if that weight moved a little, and in which direction. The list of all of them points uphill.
one number saying how wrong the network's predictions are on a set of images; training pushes it down. Also called the cost function, J.
the training rule: move every weight a small step against its gradient, so the loss goes down, then repeat. SGD (stochastic gradient descent) does it on a small random group of images at a time.
the size of each gradient-descent step, η (eta): weight change = learning rate x gradient.
the method that computes every weight's gradient: it walks backward from the loss through the layers, one layer at a time.
the slope of a curve at one point: how fast the output changes when the input changes a little. Flat curve = derivative near 0.
an activation saturates when its input is so large or so negative that the curve is flat there: pushing further barely changes the output.
gradients that shrink layer after layer on the way back, so the first layers get almost no update and stop learning.
gradients that grow layer after layer on the way back, so the weight updates become huge and training falls apart.
the family name for vanishing and exploding gradients: the gradient's size changes wildly from layer to layer.
one full pass over the training set. With 55,000 images and batches of 32, one epoch is 1,719 gradient steps.
the small group of training images used for one gradient step (Keras default: 32).
the share of images whose predicted class is the true class, e.g. 0.87 = 87% right.
the usual loss for classification: minus the log of the probability the network gave the TRUE class, so a confident wrong answer costs a lot.
Keras's step that attaches a loss, an optimizer and the metrics to a built model, before fit().
the object that turns the gradients into weight updates (plain SGD is one; lessons b06-b11 compare several). Chosen in compile().
the book's image set: 70,000 greyscale 28 x 28 photos of clothes in 10 classes (T-shirt, trouser, pullover, dress, coat, sandal, shirt, sneaker, bag, ankle boot).
using a trained network to predict (no weight changes); in Keras, predict() or calling the model with training=False.
a ReLU neuron whose weighted sum is negative for every training image: it always outputs 0, gets a 0 gradient, and never changes again.
max(alpha x z, z): like ReLU, but negative sums keep a small slope alpha (e.g. 0.2) instead of becoming 0.
Parametric ReLU: a Leaky ReLU whose slope alpha is learned in training instead of chosen by you.
exponential linear unit: z for positive sums, alpha x (e^z - 1) for negative ones, a smooth curve that settles at -alpha.
scaled ELU: an ELU times fixed constants, chosen so a plain stack of Dense layers keeps its outputs at mean 0 and std 1.
a network whose layer outputs keep mean about 0 and standard deviation about 1 on their own, with no extra normalization layer.
multilayer perceptron: a plain stack of Dense layers, nothing else.
an activation z x Phi(z), where Phi(z) is the chance a bell-curve value is below z: smooth, with a small dip below 0.
an activation z x sigmoid(z): smooth, dips slightly below 0, then rises like ReLU.
another smooth ReLU-like activation with a small dip below 0 (its curve is in Figure 11-4).
a shortcut that adds a layer's input to an output further up, skipping layers in between (Chapter 14).
a network for sequences (text, time series) that feeds its own output back in at every step (Chapter 15).
a layer that standardizes its inputs using the mean and spread of the current mini-batch, then rescales them with two learned numbers. Not the min-max normalization of Chapter 2.
a running average updated at every step that fades out old values, so it follows the recent state without storing the history.
a number stored in the model that gradient descent does not change (BN's moving averages); trainable ones (weights, gamma, beta) it does change.
storing each number in 16 bits instead of 32: half the memory, usually faster, slightly less exact.
capping the gradient before the weights are updated, so one huge gradient cannot wreck the model.
training diverges when the loss grows instead of shrinking, until the numbers become useless (often NaN, 'not a number').
the slope with respect to ONE weight while all the others are held still; the gradient is the list of them.
the ordinary length of a vector: square each component, add them up, take the square root.
TensorFlow's web page for watching a training run: loss curves, gradient sizes and more.
starting a new model from layers another model already learned on a related task, instead of from random weights.
already trained on another task, and reused as the starting point.
mark a layer's weights as not trainable (layer.trainable = False), so training leaves them alone; unfreeze = make them trainable again.
in transfer learning: keep training the reused layers with SMALL steps so they adjust to the new task. (Chapter 2's fine-tune meant choosing the best settings; this is a different use of the word.)
a model that sorts its inputs into only two classes (yes/no); here one sigmoid output gives the probability of the positive class.
first training the lower layers on unlabeled data (no answers attached), then reusing them for the labeled task.
the share of wrong predictions: 1 - accuracy. 91.85% accuracy = 8.15% error rate.
an optimizer that remembers its previous steps: the gradient changes the speed of the step instead of setting it, so steps build up speed in a consistent direction.
swing back and forth across the minimum instead of settling in it.
a long flat stretch of the loss: the gradient is tiny, so plain gradient descent crawls; also a run where the validation loss stops improving.
Nesterov accelerated gradient: momentum that measures the gradient a little ahead, where the momentum is about to carry the weights.
an optimizer that divides each weight's step by the square root of the sum of all its past squared gradients, so steep directions take smaller steps.
a step size worked out separately for every weight from its own gradient history, instead of one rate for all.
AdaGrad that forgets: it keeps a fading average of recent squared gradients instead of the sum of all of them.
the usual default optimizer: momentum (which way) plus RMSProp (how far, per weight), with a correction for its first steps.
in Adam: dividing the running averages by 1 - beta^t early on, because they start at 0 and would report values that are too small.
Adam that scales each step by the largest recent gradient size instead of the root of the average square.
Adam plus the Nesterov look-ahead; often converges a little faster.
training converges when the loss stops going down because the weights have settled.
shrinking every weight by a small fixed fraction at every step (e.g. times 0.99), so no weight grows large without a reason.
Adam with weight decay applied directly to the weights after each step, not mixed into the gradient.
adding a penalty on the weights to the loss: L2 = sum of squared weights (all shrink), L1 = sum of absolute weights (many become exactly 0).
a model in which most weights are exactly 0, so it is smaller and faster.
the table of second derivatives (how each slope changes); first-order optimizers use only the slopes (Jacobians) because Hessians are far too big.
a rule that changes the learning rate while training runs, usually from big steps to small ones.
an object you pass to fit() that Keras calls at fixed moments (start of each epoch, end of each batch) to do extra work, such as changing the learning rate.
a schedule that raises the learning rate for the first half of training, then lowers it for the second half.
an image set of 60,000 small colour photos (32 x 32) in 10 classes, such as airplane, cat and truck.
a function built inside another function that remembers the outer function's values (here lr0 and s).
a saved copy of a model (and optimizer) during or after training, so it can be reloaded and continued.
an extra amount added to the loss that grows with the weights, so large weights cost something.
at every training step, switch off a random share of the neurons (their output becomes 0) so none can rely on a particular neighbour. Off at prediction time.
two neurons co-adapt when each is only useful together with the other, a fragile arrangement that tends to memorise noise.
1 - p, the chance a neuron is NOT dropped; the surviving outputs are divided by it during training.
keep dropout ON at prediction time, predict the same image many times, and average: the spread of the answers shows how unsure the model is.
how much you should doubt a prediction; here measured as the spread of the Monte Carlo predictions.
a model is well calibrated when its probabilities match reality: of the images it gives 70%, about 70% are right.
after each training step, shrink any neuron's incoming weight vector whose length is above r back to length r.
a dropout variant that keeps the mean and spread of its inputs, so it does not break SELU's self-normalization.
how long one prediction takes, from input in to answer out.
"not a number": what a calculation returns once it has gone wrong (e.g. 0 divided by 0, or a number too big to store). Once one weight is NaN, everything it touches becomes NaN.
go past the lowest point of the loss because the step was too big or too fast, and land on the far side.
the best point: the weights where the loss is lowest (the minimum). A local optimum is lowest only compared with its neighbourhood.
the loss drawn as a surface over all possible weights: hills, valleys, flat plateaus. Training walks downhill on it.
one training step: one mini-batch in, gradients computed, weights updated once.
a table of numbers in rows and columns; a Dense layer's weights are one matrix, inputs x neurons (784 x 300 for the first layer here).
one dot of an image. A Fashion MNIST image is 28 x 28 = 784 pixels, each a brightness from 0 (black) to 255 (white), here divided by 255 to 0..1.
the size of an array along each direction; shape (100, 10000, 10) = 100 blocks of 10,000 rows of 10 numbers.
one direction of an array; axis=0 runs down the first index. .mean(axis=0) averages over it, removing that direction.
what a layer's outputs capture about the input: the pattern of numbers it hands to the next layer.
do well on NEW data, not just on the training data.
a standard test (fixed data and task) used to compare methods fairly.
a kind of deep network behind today's large language models (Chapter 16). Not Chapter 2's Scikit-Learn transformer.
stop training when the validation loss has not improved for a set number of epochs (the patience).
a network for images whose layers slide small filters over the picture (Chapter 14).
a new class built on an existing one: it gets (inherits) all its behaviour and replaces only what it redefines; super() calls the original version.
multiply by a number and add a number (a x + b): a stretch and a shift.
removing weights (setting them to 0 for good) or whole neurons that matter little, to make a network smaller and faster.
storing weights with fewer bits (e.g. 8-bit whole numbers instead of 32-bit decimals) to save memory and time.
Python's functools.partial: makes a new function from an old one with some arguments already filled in.
